headline: PAGASA Elevates Warning to Orange Level in Zambales and Bataan as Monsoon Rains Persist
seoTitle: PAGASA Keeps Orange Rainfall Warning Over Zambales and Bataan
seoDescription: PAGASA kept Zambales and Bataan under an Orange Heavy Rainfall Warning on August 14, saying flooding remained threatening as the southwest monsoon affected Luzon.
deck: PAGASA kept Zambales and Bataan under an Orange Heavy Rainfall Warning Friday morning, saying flooding remained threatening as southwest monsoon rains continued.
author: FMB News Desk

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: PAGASA kept Zambales and Bataan under an Orange Heavy Rainfall Warning at 8:00 a.m. on Friday, August 14, saying flooding remained threatening in the two provinces.

The agency's 5:00 a.m. warning had already placed Zambales and Bataan at Orange level. It also placed Pampanga, Bulacan, Metro Manila, parts of Tarlac, Cavite, Batangas, Rizal and Quezon under a Yellow warning for possible flooding in flood-prone areas.

sections.heading: Context
paragraphs: The warning identified the southwest monsoon, or Habagat, as the weather system driving the rainfall. PAGASA's regional forecast issued at 5:00 a.m. showed cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms, while the Philippine News Agency reported that rains were expected across much of Luzon.
The 8:00 a.m. update said light to moderate rain with occasional heavy rain was also affecting other parts of Southern and Central Luzon and could persist or spread to nearby areas.

sections.heading: Why this matters to Filipinos
paragraphs: An Orange warning means flooding is threatening. The notice is especially important for residents, commuters and local disaster offices in low-lying, flood-prone and landslide-prone communities across Zambales and Bataan.

sections.heading: What to watch next
paragraphs: PAGASA advised the public and disaster risk reduction offices to keep monitoring conditions and said the next regional warning was scheduled for 11:00 a.m. Residents should follow the latest PAGASA and local government instructions because warning levels can change as rainfall moves.
